w:r.w:t: The VIKZAR EMG (Electromyography) strap is a specialized, wireless data collection prototype designed to capture live neuromuscular responses from a moving athlete's quadriceps and hamstrings. The primary purpose of this device is to act as a one-time data collection and calibration tool. By capturing this data, the Vikzar team can integrate internal muscle firing metrics (effort, fatigue, imbalances) with external impact data collected by the main smart shinpad PCB.
Expected Outcome: A clinical-grade stream of raw muscle biopotentials that will enable the calculation of the
(Hamstring-to-Quadriceps) ratio, activation timing, and localized muscle fatigue. This provides the foundational dataset for true leg injury prediction.
The device leverages off-the-shelf and standard microelectronics to enable rapid prototyping.

The wiring architecture ensures clean analog readings while safely powering the system:
• Power Delivery: The 3.7V Li-Po battery is connected to the ESP32-C3 via an external sliding switch. When the switch is in the
ON position, power is supplied to the VCC/3.3V and GND pins of the MCU.
• Sensor Power: Both EMG sensors are powered directly from the ESP32-C3's 3.3V and GND output pins.
• Signal Lines (ADC1): To ensure BLE radio activity does not interfere with the readings, the sensor output signal wires are routed exclusively to ADC1 pins:
Accurate data relies on precise 3-wire electrode placement for both the Quadriceps and Hamstrings. Each sensor module uses three gel pads: Signal (MID), Reference (END), and Ground (GND).
Thickest middle part of the Rectus Femoris (front thigh).
Approx. 2 inches below the Signal pad, along the muscle fiber.
Directly on the Patella (kneecap) or side of the knee joint.
Thickest middle part of the Biceps Femoris (back thigh).
Approx. 2 inches below the Signal pad, towards the knee.
Lateral epicondyle or another bony, non-muscular area nearby.
The system relies on a dual-environment software architecture
1. Firmware (ESP32-C3): Written in C++ using the Arduino IDE. It utilizes built-in BLE libraries (`
`) to create a GATT server, read analog signals at 500Hz, pack them into byte arrays, and send them via BLE
2. Receiver Utility (Laptop/PC): Written in Python. It utilizes the `bleak` library for cross-platform Bluetooth Low Energy
` for asynchronous data handling, `struct` for unpacking byte payloads, and `matplotlib` for rendering real-time, moving graphs of the muscle activity.

The ESP32-C3 is configured to sample the analog EMG signals at a strict rate of 500 Hz per channel (500 samples per second). This high frequency is critical for capturing the fast electrical transients of muscle firing without aliasing. A 500 Hz sample rate ensures the system captures a high-fidelity waveform, which is necessary to accurately calculate the RMS (Root Mean Square) envelope and pinpoint exact muscle activation and deactivation timings during explosive movements.

The device utilizes the ESP32-C3's 12-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC), which provides a resolution of 4096 discrete steps (outputting values from 0 to 4095). When operating across the standard 3.3V logic range, a 12-bit resolution means the system can detect microscopic voltage changes as small as ~0.8 millivolts. This high sensitivity is vital for picking up the faint biopotentials generated by the quadriceps and hamstrings through the skin surface.

The system acts as a BLE GATT (Generic Attribute Profile) server. To ensure a continuous, real-time data stream without latency, the firmware packs the dual-channel 16-bit integers into optimized 20-byte payload arrays (5 samples per packet). Because 20 bytes easily fits within the default Bluetooth Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU), the radio can push these packets constantly as BLE Notifications without requiring the receiving laptop to acknowledge every single packet, preventing data bottlenecks.

The entire wearable system operates on a low-power 3.3V logic level. It is powered by a standard 3.7V Lithium-Polymer (Li-Po) battery connected via an external sliding switch. Once powered, the ESP32-C3 regulates the voltage down to 3.3V for its internal operations and radio transmission. The dual EMG sensors are extremely power-efficient and draw their required operating current directly from the microcontroller’s 3.3V and GND pins, eliminating the need for a separate power delivery circuit for the sensors.

A critical hardware limitation of the ESP32-C3 architecture is that its internal Wi-Fi/Bluetooth radio heavily shares internal resources with the ADC2 (Analog-to-Digital Converter 2) channels. If the radio is active, any analog readings taken on ADC2 pins will become corrupted or fail entirely. To bypass this limitation, the hardware design mandates that the EMG signal wires are strictly routed to ADC1 pins only (specifically GPIO 3 and GPIO 4). This guarantees clean, uninterrupted muscle readings while the BLE radio is transmitting.
The software architecture is built on the Arduino framework tailored for the
ESP32 core. Rather than using standard, blocking

Data Output: The device streams raw analog-to-digital (ADC) values ranging from 0 to 4095. This time-series data represents the
electrical firing of the muscles in real time.
The Vikzar team will utilize this data to extract critical clinical metrics:
Ratio: Comparing peak quad amplitude against peak hamstring amplitude to predict ACL injury risks.
• Activation Timing: Identifying biomechanical efficiency by seeing exactly when muscles fire during a sprint or impact.

• Future Integration: The calibrated ranges obtained from this device will be cross-referenced with the physical impact data collected by the primary smart shinpad to build holistic predictive AI models.
Step 1: Application - Clean the athlete's skin. Snap the cables onto the gel electrodes, peel the backing, and apply them to the
quads and hamstrings as per the placement guide. Wrap the strap securely to hold the hardware.
2: Power On - Slide the external battery switch to the 'ON' position to boot the ESP32-C3.
Step 3: Setup Receiver - On the laptop, ensure Bluetooth is enabled. Do not try to pair through Windows/Mac settings.
Step 4: Execute Script - Open the terminal and run the Python script (`python emg_receiver.py`).
Step 5: Monitor - The script will automatically scan, connect to 'VIKZAR_EMG_STRAP_1', and pop up a live Matplotlib window displaying the streaming muscle data.

The VIKZAR Smart Pod is a compact, BLE-enabled wearable sensor PCB module designed for retrofit testing within a wearable sports prototype enclosure (such as a compression sleeve). The primary purpose of this device is to accurately capture neuromuscular and biomechanical data during athletic movements, specifically focusing on sharp impact pulses, spatial movement, and multi-zone contact/load forces.

The device will stream live, multi-dimensional data—including load indices, contact intensity, contact durations, and high-g impacts—over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). This data will enable the Vikzar team to integrate external impact metrics with internal muscle firing data to build predictive AI models for athletic injuries and assess holistic biomechanical efficiency.
The prototype utilizes a highly integrated suite of surface-mount components, supplemented by specific external connectors and power sources to maintain an ultra-compact footprint.

The module relies on a triad of sensor inputs to provide a complete mechanical picture of the athlete's leg/impact zone:
Operating over SPI, this sensor tracks the continuous spatial movement (gait context) of the athlete.
Triggers only during severe impact events. It is linked to the MCU via hardware interrupts (INT1/INT2) to ensure that split-second hard impacts are never missed between BLE transmission cycles.
Three independent Force Sensing Resistors (FSRs) utilize RC-filtering to measure contact pressure. They do not measure exact Newtons (unless calibrated), but rather track the
Load Index, Contact Intensity, and Contact Zone
To ensure stable data pipelines and prevent radio interference, components are carefully routed to specific ESP32-S3 GPIO pins.

The system operates on a 3.3V logic level. The external 600mAh 3.7V Li-Po battery is regulated down to 3.3V by the ME6211 LDO. The battery is housed off-board in a separate foam pocket to protect the cell from direct impacts and to keep the RF keep-out area clear.

The ESP32-S3 utilizes a 12-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter, providing values from 0 to 4095, offering microscopic sensitivity to FSR voltage changes. To bypass the known architectural limitation where internal radio (Wi-Fi/BLE) usage corrupts ADC2 readings, the hardware layout specifically routes the three FSR
(IO4, IO5, IO6), guaranteeing clean readings while BLE is streaming.

The assembled PCB height must not exceed 7.5 mm to fit inside the tool-less, PETG-printed compression enclosure. Furthermore, FSR traces must be kept physically away from the power and RF antenna to prevent noise.
The software ecosystem mirrors previous Vikzar diagnostic prototypes, separated into firmware and client software:
Developed in C++ using the Arduino IDE. It uses non-blocking loops (via
)) to maintain strict high-frequency sampling (e.g., 500Hz) without crashing the Bluetooth stream. It packs the
FSR readings and IMU data into optimized 20-byte payloads to fit the standard BLE MTU size, allowing constant data flow via GATT server Notifications.
A Python-based utility utilizing the bleak library for asynchronous BLE handling and matplotlib for live, real-time data graphing.
